summary.text: An aurora is a natural light display in Earth's upper atmosphere, made when charged particles from the Sun collide with atoms there.
The collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen, which then give off light in colours such as green, red and purple.
Faster solar wind disturbs Earth's magnetosphere, sending electrons and protons down into the upper atmosphere, where they make the glow.

facts.label: Northern name
facts.value: Aurora borealis, or the northern lights

facts.label: Southern name
facts.value: Aurora australis, or the southern lights

facts.label: Usual zone
facts.value: A band about 6° wide centred on 67° latitude

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn

facts.label: Beyond Earth
facts.value: Other planets, brown dwarfs, comets and some moons

items.prompt: Curtains of green light ripple across a polar night sky. What is making the light?

options.label: Gas atoms struck by charged particles from the Sun
Sunlight bouncing off polar ice
Lightning flashing inside high clouds
Moonlight scattered by ice crystals

items.explain: Charged particles from the Sun collide with oxygen and nitrogen in the upper atmosphere, and the excited gases emit light.

items.prompt: A strong geomagnetic storm hits Earth. What happens to where people can see auroras?

options.label: They shrink to a spot over each pole
They show up much closer to the equator
They appear only in the southern sky
They vanish until the storm passes

items.explain: A geomagnetic storm makes the auroral ovals expand, bringing auroras to latitudes farther from the poles.

items.prompt: During the Carrington Event, the greatest geomagnetic storm ever observed, what did people notice in the sky?

options.label: Auroras vanished all over the world
Auroras turned a single deep blue
Auroras were seen even in the tropics
Only the southern lights stayed visible

items.explain: Storms enlarge the auroral ovals, and in the largest storm ever observed auroras reached even the tropics.

items.prompt: A bright display is lighting up the sky over Alaska. What is most likely happening in the far southern auroral zone at that moment?

options.label: Its sky stays dark until Alaska's display ends
It shows a display in the opposite colours
Nothing, since auroras happen only in the north
A near-identical display changes at the same time

items.explain: The southern lights have features almost identical to the northern lights and change at the same time as the northern auroral zone.

items.prompt: On an ordinary night with no storm, where would you have the best chance of seeing an aurora overhead?

options.label: Northern Scandinavia, near the Arctic
A beach on the equator
The Mediterranean coast
The southern United States

items.explain: Auroras are most often seen in a zone around 67° latitude, and the northern lights are visible from Arctic areas such as Scandinavia; the Mediterranean and southern US see them only on rare occasions.

items.prompt: You plan a trip to see auroras far from the poles. When do the big storms that make that possible happen most often?

options.label: During a total solar eclipse
Around the peak of the sunspot cycle
At the low point of the sunspot cycle
Only in the middle of northern winter

items.explain: Large geomagnetic storms are most common during the peak of the sunspot cycle or in the three years after it.
